# SkillPrivus: Uncovering PRIV acy of US e Harms in Agentic Skills
###### Abstract
Agent skills extend AI assistants through installable instructions and code that can access users’ files, accounts, and data. Even when performing their advertised tasks, skills may infer sensitive attributes, retain unnecessary information, or disclose data to unexpected recipients. We study these potential privacy-of-use harms through SkillPrivus, a static audit framework that analyzes skills before installation without executing them.
Applied to 726 real skills from public marketplaces, 563 of which handle personal data, SkillPrivus flags at least one potential violation in 307 of these skills (54.5%), and its judgments agree with three blind human annotators on 83.2% (κ=0.35) of resolvable moves.
## 1 Introduction
Prior work on skill-related risks has largely adopted a security perspective, examining threats such as prompt injection, tool poisoning, and data exfiltration by compromised tools (Huang et al., 2026). We focus on honest-but-negligent behavior, where a skill fulfills its stated task but infers, retains, or transmits data beyond what that task warrants, without requiring the adversarial intent of the classical honest-but-curious model.

It screens for personal-data handling, decomposes code and instructions into source-grounded *data moves*, and adapts Contextual Integrity to assess each move against the skill’s stated purpose and contextual norms. Potential privacy harms are classified using Solove’s taxonomy (Solove, 2006), which we extend with *inference* to capture newly derived sensitive attributes.

# SkillGraph: Graph Foundation Priors for LLM Agent Tool Sequence Recommendation 

Hao Liu and Dongyu Li 

Abstract —LLM agents must select tools from large API libraries and order them correctly. Existing methods use se-mantic similarity for both retrieval and ordering, but ordering depends on inter-tool data dependencies that are absent from tool descriptions. As a result, semantic-only methods can produce 

negative Kendall-τ in structured workflow domains. We intro-duce SkillGraph, a directed weighted execution-transition graph mined from 49,831 successful LLM agent trajectories, which encodes workflow-precedence regularities as a reusable graph foundation prior. Sanjiban Choudhury

Mariana Fernandez-Espinosa Ivoline Ngong Keerthiram Murugesan Karthikeyan Natesan Ramamurthy
###### Abstract

# Prior-as-Skill: Remember Outside and Read Inside with On-Policy Self-Distillation for Self-Evolving VLM Agents

arXiv:2611.15766
Authors: Yan Lin, Jingyu Sun, Yifei Qian, Zhengtao Yao, Yuxia Wang, Daizong Liu, Chun Pong Lau, Zhongliang Guo, Stephen McGough
Submitted: 2026-11-11
Subjects: cs.CV cs.AI
Comments: under review

Abstract

Self-evolving visual agents keep what they learn as skills: key frames with step notes on a task's steps and their order. On-policy self-distillation (OPSD) is now a popular way to train such skills into a vision-language model that matches, on its own answers, a teacher that also reads the written order. At deployment, frames often go missing or show an unusual order, as when a person or a website reorders the steps. Existing internalization methods keep any order they store in the frame-reading weights: trained on full frames, the model guesses when they are missing, and trained with frames withheld, it stores the order, so memory can override what it sees. We propose PriorSplit, which fills in missing frames from an order kept outside the model, with no training beyond OPSD. It counts which of two neighboring steps comes first in training episodes, and the model checks if both asked steps are in view: if so, it answers from the frames, and otherwise the counts answer. Extensive experiments on synthetic skills with five models and on step-tagged order questions in new episodes of seen web, cooking and egocentric tasks demonstrate that, with frames missing, PriorSplit outperforms every compared method at OPSD's training cost.

###### Abstract

Agent skills extend AI assistants through installable instructions and code that can access users’ files, accounts, and data. Even when performing their advertised tasks, skills may infer sensitive attributes, retain unnecessary information, or disclose data to unexpected recipients. We study these potential privacy-of-use harms through SkillPrivus , a static audit framework that analyzes skills before installation without executing them. SkillPrivus extracts data operations from code and natural-language instructions, grounds them in source evidence, and adapts Contextual Integrity to assess their appropriateness. SkillPrivus finds privacy risks in 307 of 563 AI agent skills

The tool found a possible violation in 54.5 percent of the skills that use personal data, and it did this before installation.
Researchers made SkillPrivus, a tool that reads an agent skill before installation and does not operate it. A skill is a set of instructions and code that gives an AI assistant new functions. The team tested 726 skills from open marketplaces. Of 563 skills that use personal data, 307 had at least 1 possible privacy violation.

How it works

SkillPrivus gets data operations from the code and from the text instructions. It connects each one to its position in the source. Then it checks if the use of the data is correct for its context.

The numbers

The tool found a possible violation in 54.5 percent of the 563 skills. Its results agree with 3 blind human annotators in 83.2 percent of the items that have a clear answer.

What is not known

The marked items are possible violations, not shown damage. The paper does not tell how many skills cause damage in use. The behaviors are sensitive inferences, use of data for more than the task of the skill, and disclosure to other recipients.

Insight: Skills can break privacy while they do their task

The paper tells that the damage comes from the functions that skills have, not from attacks. An earlier tool makes open records of agent work, and one more tool lets agents read software on the machine of the user. This reads as a race: tools that record agents and give them more functions move at a higher speed than checks of the data use of skills. A check before installation can become a gate.
Why it made the cut
For teams that let staff install agent skills: make a list of the skills with access to files and accounts, and examine the ones that use personal data first.
